title: Focal Segmental Glomerulosclerosis
subject: Pathology
summary: A podocyte disease causing nephrotic syndrome, often steroid‑resistant. Diagnosis rests on biopsy showing focal, segmental sclerosis. Management focuses on treating the underlying cause and supportive care.

sections.p: FSGS is a podocytopathy where some glomeruli (focal) show sclerosis limited to part of the tuft (segmental). It is the leading cause of nephrotic syndrome in adults, especially in Black populations.

t.b: Confirms focal, segmental sclerosis and rules out other glomerulopathies; a key diagnostic step when nephrotic syndrome is steroid‑resistant or atypical.

sections.p: Staging follows KDIGO: Stage 1 (eGFR ≥90), Stage 2 (60–89), Stage 3 (30–59), Stage 4 (15–29), Stage 5 (<15). Proteinuria categories: <3.5 g/24h (non‑nephrotic), 3.5–10 g/24h (nephrotic), >10 g/24h (super‑nephrotic).

sections.p: Primary FSGS is idiopathic, often linked to genetic mutations (NPHS2, ACTN4). Secondary causes common in low‑resource settings include HIV, hepatitis B, schistosomiasis, malaria, sickle cell, and herbal nephrotoxins.

sections.p: Patients present with edema (periorbital, pedal), frothy urine, weight gain, and hypertension. Early stages may be asymptomatic; advanced disease shows oliguria and rising creatinine.

Hypertension is common and worsens renal outcomes.

sections.p: Treat the underlying cause first. Supportive care includes ACE/ARB for proteinuria, diuretics for edema, statins for dyslipidaemia, and infection control. Steroids are first line for presumed primary FSGS but many patients are steroid‑resistant; alternatives include calcineurin inhibitors (cyclosporine, tacrolimus) or mycophenolate mofetil.

t.b: Reduces intraglomerular pressure, slows proteinuria; avoid if serum potassium >5.5 mmol/L.

sections.p: Regular monitoring of proteinuria, eGFR, BP, and serum albumin every 3–6 months. Counsel on salt restriction, avoid nephrotoxins, and ensure vaccinations (HepB, pneumococcal).

faq.q: Is HIV treatment enough to control FSGS?
faq.a: Antiretroviral therapy can reduce proteinuria but many patients still need immunosuppression.

exam: What is the most useful test to confirm FSGS? — Renal biopsy showing focal, segmental sclerosis and no immune deposits.
Which drug class is preferred for steroid‑resistant FSGS? — Calcineurin inhibitors (cyclosporine or tacrolimus).
Why should ACE inhibitors be avoided if serum potassium is high? — They can raise potassium further, risking hyperkalaemia.
What is the first step if a patient with nephrotic syndrome develops pulmonary oedema? — Immediate diuretic therapy and assessment for fluid overload.
How does HIV infection contribute to FSGS? — Direct podocyte injury via viral proteins and immune dysregulation.
What laboratory finding would argue against primary FSGS? — Low complement levels (C3/C4).
When should a nephrologist be consulted in a low‑resource setting? — When proteinuria >3.5 g/24h or rapid decline in eGFR.
